source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs (IEEE CogMI)
finding: Reasoning models are not less biased than matched non-reasoning siblings. The point estimate leans the wrong way in every family, but the pooled test is not reliable.
numbers: 30 vignettes, 6 biases (5 items each) from the Malberg benchmark; 7 models in 4 families (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen3 thinking/instruct); ceilings 0/1,024/4,096/8,192 thinking tokens; 12,350 calls, 10 samples per cell at T=1.0. Pooled reasoning minus sibling bias magnitude Delta=+0.031, 95% CI [-0.010,+0.074], t(29)=1.45, p=.157, dz=0.27.
quote: longer thinking should weaken the classic decision biases that fast, intuitive judgment produces. We test that prediction.
limits: Only 5 items per bias, so item-level tests are weak. DeepSeek and Qwen cannot turn thinking off, so their comparison crosses a model boundary. Small, mostly 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: reasoning-trained models do not buy a bias fix on judgement items. Do not assume that a thinking mode removes anchoring or framing.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs (IEEE CogMI) (dose-response result)
finding: More realised thinking did not reduce bias. No model had a significantly negative slope of bias magnitude on realised reasoning tokens. Where anything moved, the signed score drifted further from the human direction.
numbers: Slope of |s| per doubling of realised tokens: Claude +0.0029 (t(29)=0.91, p=.372; realised range 0-805 tokens); GPT-5.1 +0.0084 (p=.018; range only 0-225); DeepSeek-R1 p=.958 (707-2,807 tokens); Qwen3 p=.213 (534-3,440). Signed drift: Claude -0.0059 (p=.018), GPT-5.1 -0.0104 (p=.010). Requested ceiling was not realised: Claude used mean 437/575/620 tokens at the three ceilings; GPT-5.1 used 116-118 tokens whatever the ceiling.
limits: Realised thinking ranges are short (under 3,500 tokens); a much larger budget is untested. Five items per bias. Bias score is a signed shift on an ordinal scale, not task accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: extra thinking budget at fixed cost does not reduce anchoring or framing in these models. Log tokens actually used, not the ceiling requested.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs (IEEE CogMI) (bias taxonomy)
finding: Only anchoring points in the human direction. Framing, loss aversion, escalation and confirmation lean the opposite way in all seven models. This partly departs from earlier benchmark papers.
numbers: Signed score vs 0 over 85 cells, Holm-corrected: anchoring +0.163 [+0.111,+0.215] d=1.89 pHolm=.037 (range +0.11 Qwen3-thinking to +0.20 Claude instruct); framing -0.336 d=-2.35 pHolm=.010 (reversed); escalation -0.070, confirmation -0.139, loss aversion -0.586 (directional, pHolm .197-.256); availability -0.035 (absent).
limits: Differs from Malberg 2024 and Knipper 2025 (where reasoning models resist framing); authors cannot say whether sampling 10 responses at T=1, item choice or newer models explain it. Signed-shift metric.
agent_relevance: Do not apply human-bias fixes blindly. Test each bias in the target model first; a fix for a bias the model does not show can add error.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs (IEEE CogMI) (verbalise-the-anchor line)
finding: One prompt line (restate every number in the prompt before answering) lowered anchoring on all 5 anchoring items, which no amount of extra thinking did. The effect is directional, not significant.
numbers: Pooled change -0.015, 95% CI [-0.026,-0.004] over cells; item level t(4)=-2.65, p=.057; sign test 5 of 5, p=.063; 5 of 7 models improved (per-model change from -0.068 to +0.032).
quote: A single prompt line moved anchoring the helpful way on every item
limits: Five items, one bias, one prompt wording. Not replicated.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: this is an input-restructuring step (bring the anchor into view), not a general reminder. It fits the finding that changing the input beats adding warnings (K16).

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering (PROBE-SWE) (RQ1 baselines)
finding: Common prompt fixes did not reliably cut bias sensitivity. Chain of thought was worse than no strategy. Self-debiasing wording helped a little but not significantly per bias.
numbers: Mean bias sensitivity (answer flips between matched biased and unbiased dilemma): no strategy 12.9%; CoT 16.1%; implication prompt 13.3%; impersonated self-debias 10.2%; imperative self-debias 10.3%; both 8.3% (-4.6 points). After FDR correction no bias-family comparison significant (all p>=.07). 6 models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B; 8 SE biases.
limits: Cheap and open models only, no frontier reasoning model; sensitivity is a flip rate, not accuracy. Baseline sensitivity range by bias 5.9% (anchoring) to 35.3% (hindsight).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and K14: generic reflection and CoT prompts are weak and can hurt. This matches schema 4b (no generic reminder).

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering (PROBE-SWE) (RQ2 axiomatic cues)
finding: Making the implicit best-practice rules explicit before answering (the model first lists facts, rules and background axioms, then answers) cut bias sensitivity about 51% on average. This is a missing-rule fix, and it worked where generic prompts did not.
numbers: Sensitivity: no strategy ~12.9%; sAX+BW and sAX+BW+IsD ~6.3% (p<.001 after Benjamini-Hochberg); sAX ~7.2% (p<.01); 2sAX+BW ~7.5% (p<.01); ProbeAX ~7.6%. Rank-biserial effect ~.4-.5. Up to 73% reduction for some biases; hindsight was an outlier.
limits: Same cheap models; rules are SE best practices the authors wrote or elicited; no compute match against best-of-N (extra elicitation call). Aggregated over biases, per-bias power is limited.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: first LLM evidence that supplying or eliciting the missing rule works where reminders fail. Candidate operator: elicit rules first, then decide. Needs a split by bias type, which this paper does not provide.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering (PROBE-SWE) (open-ended check and real-use prevalence)
finding: The axiom fix carries over to open-ended answers, but the effect is smaller and uncertain. Explicit bias cues are rare in real developer prompts.
numbers: 40 open-ended dilemmas per model: GPT-4o-mini 0.40 to 0.275 (-12.5 points, ~31% relative; bootstrap CI [-10.0,35.0] points); Llama-3.1-8B 0.40 to 0.30 (-10 points, ~25%; CI [-7.5,27.5]). Coder agreement 80.0% (kappa .55) for Llama and 82.5% (kappa .62) for GPT. In DevGPT, 97 of 5,269 coding prompts (1.84%) had an explicit bias cue.
limits: Small n, CIs include zero; manual coding of free text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: with 40 items per arm, a 10-12 point gain has a CI that spans zero. Plan at least 100-200 matched items per arm for a detectable gain of this size.

source: Hills (2025) Could you be wrong: Debiasing LLMs using a metacognitive prompt for improving human decision making
finding: Gap 5: this is the nearest thing to a prompt-level pre-mortem, and it is a demonstration, not a test. After an answer, the prompt 'could you be wrong?' makes the model list errors, biases and alternatives it did not state before.
numbers: No effect sizes, no sample, no control arm. Examples taken from published LLM-bias questions plus one incomplete-information case.
quote: Could you be wrong prompts the LLM to identify its own biases and produce cogent metacognitive reflection.
limits: Qualitative only. It shows the model can produce critique when asked, not that the final answer becomes more accurate.
agent_relevance: Cannot count as evidence that pre-mortem works. Test it: pre-answer failure-listing vs post-answer 'could you be wrong' vs none, at equal tokens.

source: Kim, Kim, Park, Park, Breazeal, McDuff, Park (2025) InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models
finding: Gap 5 (analogue only): a structured pre-answer step (enumerate harms, analyse consequences, answer under constraints) lowered harmful output in prompting and in training. It targets safety, not human-style judgement bias.
numbers: Up to 32% reduction in harmfulness vs zero-shot and 16% vs SafetyPrompt in professional-ethics and agentic-misalignment scenarios; reasoning benchmarks preserved after training (SFT and GRPO, three model families). Prompt-only numbers per model were not extracted in this session.
limits: Outcome is harmfulness, not anchoring or framing. Name 'premortem' is used by the authors; no human prospective-hindsight control.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a failure-first step at answer time. Not evidence on cognitive-bias reduction.

source: Bahaj, Rahimi, Chetouani, Ghogho (2025) Gauging Overprecision in LLMs: An Empirical Study
finding: Gap 7: LLMs are overprecise on numeric interval questions. Hit rate does not rise when the prompt asks for a higher confidence level, and interval length does not track the stated level.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini; FinQA, medical MCQ-derived and MMLU numeric questions; levels 60/70/80/90/95%, 5 trials each, 10 simulation runs. GPT-4o-mini vanilla hit-average: FinQA 18.29%, Medical 60.30%, MMLU 68.04% (nominal 60-95%). GPT-3.5 FinQA hit rate 5.50% at 90% vs 7.42% at 60%.
limits: Only two models, both old or small; numeric answers filtered to unit-free numbers. This is not the SPIES method.
agent_relevance: Asking for 'a 90% interval' does not calibrate the agent. A different elicitation format must be tested.

source: Bahaj, Rahimi, Chetouani, Ghogho (2025) Gauging Overprecision in LLMs: An Empirical Study (CoT and refinement)
finding: CoT improved interval hit rate for GPT-4o-mini but not for GPT-3.5. Aggregating several sampled intervals helped a little, and self-refinement mostly made things worse, unlike human results with others' estimates.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini hit-average vanilla to CoT: MMLU 68.04% to 80.49%, Medical 60.30% to 67.47%, FinQA 18.29% to 20.19%. GPT-3.5: MMLU 59.35% to 58.30%, FinQA 6.47% to 7.29%. Union aggregation helped mainly by widening intervals.
limits: Higher hit rate with wider intervals is not better calibration by itself. No SPIES bins, no fractile split, no frontier model.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no LLM test of SPIES or fractile (10th/50th/90th) elicitation. Haran et al. (a17) human result is untested for LLMs.

source: Shen et al. (2026) RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data?
finding: Gap 6 (negative side): carrying forward the agent's own stored insights from earlier windows induced anchoring. Removing the insight memory improved action recommendations.
numbers: Qwen3-235B action-recommendation Hit@5 0.526 with insight memory vs 0.601 without. Agent keeps ~6 hypotheses per patient, 80% with anticipatory exceptions. Recall-safety trade-off: up to 47.3% of recommendations flagged potentially harmful.
limits: ICU domain, one benchmark (94 patients gold, 930 windows); anchoring is judged in hindsight by physicians and by an LLM labeller for the larger set.
agent_relevance: A memory of past interpretations is not a free debiaser. A memory of past errors and corrections needs a test that separates it from a memory of past conclusions.

source: Shen et al. (2026) RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data? (ICU-Evo structured memory)
finding: Structured memory (recent observations, trends, critical events, summaries, insights) improved long-horizon reasoning but did not remove unsafe recommendations; the weak spot was again premature anchoring on red-flag actions.
numbers: ICU-Evo up to +0.268 over RAG on Acute Problems Hit for Gemini-3.1-pro; three backbones tested (Gemini-3.1-pro, GPT-5.4, Qwen3-235B). Red Flag harm rate remained the weak point.
limits: No explicit past-error feedback arm; no transfer to untrained bias facets tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: no study mimics game-with-feedback training by retrieving past errors and testing transfer.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Judging with Many Minds: Do More Perspectives Mean Less Prejudice?
finding: Gap 8: same-model multi-agent debate raised bias in LLM judges after the first round and the elevated bias persisted; a meta-judge over several judges resisted better.
numbers: Four biases (position, verbosity, CoT, bandwagon) on MTBench and CALM-Alignment; judge models including R1-Distilled-Qwen 32B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek-V3. Paired t-tests: significant drop in consistency from round 0 to round 1 across judge-critic pairs; no further drop or recovery in rounds 2-3.
limits: LLM-as-judge bias, not decision bias. Consistency scores, not accuracy; no token match vs single agent.
agent_relevance: Debate with same-model agents is risky for bias. Supports 4b (do not add debate).

source: Ma et al. (2025) Judging with Many Minds: Do More Perspectives Mean Less Prejudice? (bias-free agent)
finding: Adding one debiased agent (PINE) as critic reduced position bias in debate, with small gains; it helped less in the meta-judge setup. Diversity from one debiased voice is not the same as role diversity.
numbers: Position consistency with PINE critic rises over rounds: GPT-4o-mini judge MTBench 0.817, 0.825, 0.831; CALM 0.786, 0.804, 0.815. Llama3.3 70B judge MTBench 0.802, 0.812, 0.821; CALM 0.781, 0.786, 0.788.
limits: Gains of 0.01-0.03; PINE is a single-agent debiaser tied to position bias; DReaMAD/MoLaCE role-diversity designs not compared in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no equal-token head-to-head of role-diverse debate vs a single debiased agent.

source: Martey, Shaw, Stromer-Galley, Kenski, Clegg, Folkestad, Saulnier, Strzalkowski (2014) Testing the Power of Game Lessons: The Effects of Art and Narrative on Reducing Cognitive Biases (DiGRA)
finding: Gap 3: independent test of game-based bias training (different game, different labs from Morewedge). The game beat a professionally made video at once and after 8 weeks, for fundamental attribution error (FAE) and confirmation bias (CB). It did not beat the video for bias blind spot.
numbers: 2x2 game (narrative x art) plus video; immediate post N=391 game participants (pre-post analysis) plus 89 video. Combined bias score pre to post: LN/MA 19.91 to 2.44; LN/DA 22.37 to 5.11; RN/MA 19.70 to -0.61; RN/DA 21.04 to 3.67; video 18.65 to 14.82. Game vs video t(475)=-5.26 (FAE) and t(475)=-4.61 (CB), p<.0005; bias blind spot t(475)=-0.19, ns. Pre-to-post across game cells Wilks lambda=.48, F(3,390)=426.50.
limits: Not a no-training control; the comparator is a video. Scores are combined bias-test scores, not real decisions. Same program (IARPA SIRIUS) as Morewedge, so the independence is of teams and games, not of funder.
agent_relevance: Supports K03: the finding that a game with practice beats passive instruction is not from one lab. Transfer to real decisions still untested.

source: Martey, Shaw, Stromer-Galley, Kenski, Clegg, Folkestad, Saulnier, Strzalkowski (2014) Testing the Power of Game Lessons: The Effects of Art and Narrative on Reducing Cognitive Biases (DiGRA) (8-week retention)
finding: At 8 weeks the game still beat the video on FAE. For CB there was no game advantage over video at retention. Retention samples are much smaller than the post-test samples.
numbers: Combined bias score at 8 weeks: LN/MA 10.46 (N=30), LN/DA 11.42 (N=36), RN/MA 6.70 (N=40), RN/DA 8.17 (N=38), video 17.36 (N=40), against pre-test means 18.65-22.37. Pre-to-retention game conditions Wilks lambda=.64. FAE game vs video t(179)=-2.45, p<.05; CB t(179)=1.37, ns.
limits: Heavy attrition (144 retention participants in the game cells vs 391 at post-test); retained participants may differ. Part of the gain decays by 8 weeks (post-test means about 0-5, retention about 7-11).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: independent replication of the short-term and 8-week effect, with decay; no test beyond 8 weeks found.

source: Dunbar et al. (2017) Mitigation of Cognitive Bias with a Serious Game (Int. J. Game-Based Learning)
finding: Another team's serious-game studies on feedback design. Game beat a professional training video; longer feedback and repeats helped; just-in-time and delayed feedback did not differ; computer feedback beat feedback from other players. Abstract only was read.
numbers: Two studies; no numbers read this session.
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref). Dunbar 2014 (Computers in Human Behavior, implicit vs explicit training) and Clegg et al. 2015 (Procedia Manufacturing) could not be opened (publisher redirects).
agent_relevance: Feedback source and timing are design variables for any memory-feedback loop: machine-generated feedback was at least as good as peer feedback.

source: Anon. (2026) Investigating Anchoring Bias and Prompt-Based Mitigation in Large Language Models (Oxford J. of Student Scholarship, vol 10 issue 3)
finding: Gap 2 and 10: prompt fixes work for some models and not others. Explicit debiasing helped Mistral-Large-3 only; estimate-first prompting helped DeepSeek-V3.1 only; baseline differences between models were not significant.
numbers: 24 monetary estimation items, high and low anchor versions; 3 models (Mistral-Large-3, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama-3.1-8B); paired t-tests on normalised percent difference. Abstract page only; PDF numbers not read.
limits: Student journal, small item set, abstract only, high prompt-level variance.
agent_relevance: Shows that the same prompt fix changes sign of effect by model; test per model.

source: Kraishan (2026) and Sovrano et al. (2026) read together: sample size and unit of analysis (our reading)
finding: Gap 10: with few items per bias, the item is the unit that matters, not the number of calls. Kraishan ran 12,350 calls but only 30 items, and the anchor-restating effect (5 of 5 items) stayed at p=.057.
numbers: Kraishan: 5 items per bias, 10 samples per cell, T=1.0; t(4) tests. PROBE-SWE open-ended arm: 40 items per model, CIs about 35 points wide. Rule of thumb from these two: 5 items cannot reach p<.05 for a gain of 0.015 on the score scale; 40 items cannot exclude zero for a 10-12 point gain.
limits: Our synthesis, not a power analysis from the authors. Paraphrase variance (Suri, Macmillan-Scott) was not re-measured here.
agent_relevance: Test plan: many items per bias (100 or more), paraphrase sets, 10 or more repeats, analysis at item level with paired tests.
